title: Which super products failed APRA’s performance test?
full_text:
The annual superannuation performance test conducted by APRA has recorded the first MySuper failure since 2023, with a total of 12 products failing to meet the 2026 benchmark.
APRA assessed 547 superannuation products representing 61 per cent of member benefits across the sector.
Among the 50 MySuper products assessed, BUSSQ’s Balanced Growth MySuper investment option was the sole failure, representing around 66,500 member accounts and $6.4 billion in assets as at 30 June 2026.
Platform products accounted for the remaining 11 of the 12 failures, with 130 of the 141 platform TDPs assessed passing the test.
BUSSQ acknowledged the result was its first failure and stressed it did not change members’ access to their super, with the product remaining open to both new and existing members.
BUSSQ chief executive, Damian Wills, said the fund had taken the result seriously and had already been working to improve member outcomes.
“We acknowledge and understand the importance of the performance test in providing transparency for members. It does not affect the security of members’ savings, and our Balanced Growth MySuper product remains open to new and existing members.”
The fund said it had implemented targeted measures to improve investment returns, with the Balanced Growth option recording top-quartile quarterly returns to the end of July 2026.
Wills said BUSSQ had conducted a holistic review of its investment strategy last year and subsequently made material changes to its portfolio.
“Our priority is, and always has been, delivering strong retirement outcomes for our members. We conducted a holistic review of our investment strategy last year and implemented material changes to our investment strategy and portfolio, removing underperforming investment managers and moving to more indexed equity mandates.
“We encourage members to speak with us if they need help. We are committed to being transparent with members and will keep them informed as we make further improvements”, said Wills.
APRA chair John Lonsdale said the results showed areas of underperformance remained despite the impact of the test since its introduction in 2021.
“The annual performance test has been effective at reducing the number of members in underperforming products over the past five years. However, this year’s results show that pockets of underperformance remain and reinforce the need for trustees to take timely and effective action.”
Platform products accounted for 11 of the 12 failures, with 130 of the 141 platform TDPs assessed passing the test.
The failed platform products represented around 4,800 member accounts and $700 million in assets. Six were first-time failures, while five had failed for at least two consecutive years, representing around $300 million in assets.
APRA’s underlying product data showed the failures included products with exposure to MLC MultiActive High Growth and MLC MultiActive Geared investment options across a number of Insignia Financial-related platforms.
Insignia confirmed MLC MultiActive High Growth and MLC MultiActive Geared had failed the test across three super funds within its Wrap platform business. Together, members invested in the two options represented approximately 0.18 per cent of its overall membership.
The wealth manager said all options in its Master Trust business passed alongside the overwhelming majority of investment options within its Wrap business.
Despite failing the test, MLC MultiActive High Growth delivered a net return of 8.84 per cent over one year and 9.68 per cent per annum over 10 years to 30 June 2026. MLC MultiActive Geared returned 10.16 per cent over one year and 12.04 per cent per annum over 10 years.
Insignia argued the characteristics of specialised investment options could result in a mismatch with the benchmarks underpinning the test.
“These options are specifically designed for members seeking higher growth and, as a result, have greater exposure to share markets, particularly high-growth equities. While that approach can deliver strong long-term outcomes, it may not always align perfectly with the benchmarks used in the Performance Test.”
Other platform failures identified in APRA’s data included products linked to Bendigo Superannuation Pty Ltd and N. M. Superannuation Proprietary Limited, with the five consecutive failures concentrated among those two trustees.
Bendigo SmartStart Super products linked to the Bendigo Balanced Wholesale Fund and Bendigo High Growth Index Fund were among the repeat failures.
Products offered by N. M. Superannuation Proprietary Limited were also among the consecutive failures, including products linked to the North Guardian Balanced Fund, North Guardian Growth Fund and North Guardian Moderately Defensive Fund.
Other first-time platform failures were associated with Oasis Fund Management Limited and OnePath Custodians Pty Limited, including products with exposure to MLC MultiActive Geared Trust and MLC MultiActive High Growth Trust.
Across the 12 failures, six trustees were responsible for the underperforming products. APRA said poorer investment performance, rather than higher administration fees and costs, was largely responsible for the failures.
Insignia said the results demonstrated limitations in applying the performance test to specialised investment options on wrap platforms.
“While we fully support the objective of helping Australians compare superannuation products, this outcome highlights some of the limitations of applying the Performance Test to specialised investment options on Wrap platforms. We will continue to work constructively with the Government and Treasury on this matter to ensure more representative results for our members.”
Alongside the test results, APRA released its 2026 Comprehensive Product Performance Package, which provides additional measures of investment returns and fees across the sector.
The regulator found administration fees had continued to decline across all product types, although platform TDPs remained materially more expensive even before personal advice costs were considered.
Platform TDPs also had higher rates of underperformance over 10 years compared with other product types, according to APRA.
“Lower administration fees can make a meaningful difference to members’ retirement balances by supporting higher net returns,” Lonsdale said. “APRA expects trustees to maintain a close focus on administration fees and fund performance in the best financial interests of their fund members.”
APRA noted the government was considering options to strengthen the performance test, with regard to promoting productivity and protecting member interests.
